subject: bio
title: Infectious Diseases
subtitle: Pathogens, transmission, control and global health.
concept: Pathogens include bacteria, viruses, fungi and protoctists; each causes disease by different mechanisms.
Transmission can be direct or indirect; breaking the chain of transmission is key to controlling infectious diseases.
Global efforts (WHO, vaccines, antibiotics) have reduced mortality but drug resistance and emerging diseases remain challenges.

notes.heading: Types of Pathogen
items: Bacteria: prokaryotes; some produce toxins (e.g. Vibrio cholerae produces cholera toxin; Mycobacterium tuberculosis causes TB).
Viruses: non-cellular; hijack host cell machinery to replicate; e.g. HIV, influenza, measles.
Fungi: e.g. Candida (thrush); Tinea (athlete's foot). Can produce spores for transmission.
Protoctists: eukaryotic; e.g. Plasmodium (malaria — transmitted by Anopheles mosquito — female vector).

notes.heading: Transmission
items: Direct contact: physical touch (e.g. STIs), droplets (TB, influenza, COVID-19).
Indirect: vectors (mosquito → malaria), contaminated water (cholera, typhoid), contaminated food, fomites (contaminated surfaces).
Cholera: Vibrio cholerae in contaminated water → toxin causes Cl⁻ secretion into intestine lumen → osmotic water loss → severe diarrhoea.
TB: Mycobacterium tuberculosis; airborne droplets; can be latent; BCG vaccine provides protection.
Malaria: Plasmodium falciparum (most dangerous); female Anopheles mosquito vector; infects liver and RBCs.

notes.heading: Control Measures
items: Vaccination (herd immunity: when enough of population is immune, spread is halted even among unvaccinated).
Antibiotics: effective against bacteria; not viruses. Antibiotic resistance: mutations in bacteria; selection pressure from misuse.
Water treatment and sanitation: cholera control.
Quarantine and contact tracing: limiting direct transmission.
WHO: coordinates global health responses; monitors disease outbreaks.

notes.heading: Drug Resistance
items: Antibiotic resistance arises by natural selection: random mutation → resistant bacterium → selective advantage → spreads.
Multi-drug resistant TB (MDR-TB): requires longer, more toxic treatment.
Strategies: complete courses of antibiotics; rotate antibiotic types; prescribe only when necessary.

definitions.body: A microorganism or agent that causes disease.
An organism that transmits a pathogen from one host to another without itself being the cause of disease.
Indirect protection of unvaccinated individuals when a sufficient proportion of the population is immune, reducing pathogen transmission.
The ability of bacteria to survive exposure to antibiotics due to mutations; arises through natural selection under antibiotic selective pressure.

workedExamples.q: Explain how antibiotic resistance arises in a bacterial population.

steps.text: A random mutation in a bacterium's DNA produces a change that confers resistance to the antibiotic (e.g. altered target protein, enzyme that breaks down the antibiotic).
When antibiotics are used, non-resistant bacteria are killed; the resistant bacterium survives and reproduces (natural selection — antibiotic is the selection pressure).
The resistant bacterium passes on its resistance gene to daughter cells (vertical transmission) and to other bacteria (horizontal gene transfer via plasmids). The resistant strain spreads.

mistakes: Stating antibiotics kill viruses — antibiotics only work on bacteria (target bacterial cell walls, ribosomes, etc.).
Describing the mosquito as the 'cause' of malaria — the mosquito is the vector; Plasmodium is the pathogen.
Confusing herd immunity (indirect protection) with direct immunity from vaccination.
tips: For malaria questions: female Anopheles mosquito is the vector; Plasmodium is the protoctist pathogen.
Cholera mechanism: toxin → Cl⁻ out of epithelial cells → water follows by osmosis → diarrhoea.
Link antibiotic resistance to natural selection — use the correct terminology: variation, selection pressure, survival, reproduction, inheritance.

flashcards.q: What type of pathogen causes malaria, and how is it transmitted?
flashcards.a: Plasmodium (a protoctist); transmitted by the bite of an infected female Anopheles mosquito.

flashcards.q: Why are antibiotics ineffective against viral infections?
flashcards.a: Antibiotics target bacterial structures (e.g. cell wall, 70S ribosome) that viruses do not have — viruses use host cell machinery.
When a high enough proportion of the population is immune to a disease, transmission is reduced enough to protect even unvaccinated individuals.

flashcards.q: How does Vibrio cholerae cause diarrhoea?
flashcards.a: Cholera toxin causes Cl⁻ ions to be secreted into the intestinal lumen; water follows by osmosis → massive watery diarrhoea → dehydration.

flashcards.q: Describe how antibiotic resistance spreads between bacteria.
flashcards.a: Via plasmid transfer (horizontal gene transfer / conjugation) or vertically by binary fission; selection pressure from antibiotic use favours resistant strains.

flashcards.q: What is the BCG vaccine and what does it protect against?
flashcards.a: BCG (Bacillus Calmette–Guérin) is a live attenuated vaccine that provides protection against tuberculosis (TB).

questions.exp: Malaria is caused by the protoctist Plasmodium — most dangerous species is P. falciparum.
Cholera is spread via water contaminated with Vibrio cholerae — a faecal-oral route.

questions.q: Why should a full course of antibiotics be completed?
opts: To ensure all bacteria are killed, reducing chance of resistance developing
questions.exp: Stopping early leaves the most resistant bacteria alive to reproduce and spread.

questions.q: What is the role of the female Anopheles mosquito in malaria?
opts: It is the vector that transmits Plasmodium
questions.exp: The female Anopheles mosquito is the vector — it transmits Plasmodium when it takes a blood meal.

A bacterium resistant to methicillin/many antibiotics
A drug used to treat TB
questions.exp: MRSA (methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus) is a bacterium that has developed resistance to many antibiotics, common in healthcare settings.
